title: Week 9 · Lesson 25: Psychiatric Pathophysiology & Clinical Reasoning — FNP-Level Approach
html:
PHASE 1 · ADVANCED PATHOPHYSIOLOGY + CLINICAL REASONING

Week 9 — Lesson 25: Psychiatric Pathophysiology & Clinical Reasoning

FNP-level goal: Evaluate mood, anxiety, psychotic, substance-related, and cognitive presentations using biopsychosocial reasoning; rule out urgent medical mimics; and recognize when suicide risk, psychosis, mania, intoxication/withdrawal, or inability to care for self requires emergency action.

Learning Objectives

  • Differentiate depressive, manic/hypomanic, anxiety, psychotic, delirium, and substance-related syndromes.
  • Use a focused mental-status examination and safety assessment.
  • Identify medical and medication causes that can mimic psychiatric illness.
  • Recognize suicide-risk warning signs and emergency-disposition thresholds.

Part 1 — A Psychiatric Symptom Is Not Automatically a Psychiatric Diagnosis

Sleep change, anxiety, low mood, hallucinations, agitation, poor concentration, and behavior change can arise from primary psychiatric illness, substance intoxication/withdrawal, medication effects, endocrine disease, infection, hypoxia, neurologic disease, pain, trauma, or metabolic disturbance. First ask: Is this acute? Is there delirium, intoxication, withdrawal, psychosis, mania, or immediate safety risk?

FNP reasoning integrates biology, psychological stressors, trauma, social supports, housing/food security, culture, medical comorbidity, medications, and substance use without assuming symptoms are “all in the patient’s head.”

Part 2 — The Mental Status Examination

Document appearance, behavior, psychomotor activity, speech, mood, affect, thought process, thought content, perception, cognition, insight, judgment, and safety. A patient may say mood is “fine” while affect, function, sleep, behavior, and collateral history suggest severe illness.

Thought process asks how ideas connect: linear, tangential, disorganized, racing, or slowed. Thought content asks what is present: hopelessness, delusions, obsessions, suicidal or homicidal thoughts, and plans. Perception includes hallucinations and misperceptions.

Part 3 — Depression and Anxiety

Major depression is more than transient sadness; it involves a persistent syndrome with impaired function and may include low mood or anhedonia, sleep/appetite change, low energy, guilt, psychomotor change, impaired concentration, and thoughts of death. Anxiety disorders involve excessive fear/worry and physiologic arousal, but chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, tremor, and insomnia also require medical and substance/medication assessment.

Ask about bipolar-spectrum history before treating a depressive presentation as unipolar depression. A history of distinct elevated/irritable episodes, decreased need for sleep, increased goal-directed activity, impulsivity, grandiosity, or pressured speech changes the diagnostic and treatment pathway.

Part 4 — Mania, Hypomania, and Psychosis

Mania can include abnormally elevated or irritable mood, decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, racing thoughts, grandiosity, distractibility, increased activity, and risky behavior with major functional impairment. Severe episodes can include psychosis and loss of judgment.

Psychosis may include delusions, hallucinations, disorganized thinking, or grossly disorganized behavior. It can occur in schizophrenia-spectrum illness, mood disorders, substance-related conditions, delirium, neurologic illness, and medical disease. New-onset psychosis, fluctuating attention, abnormal vital signs, focal deficits, or late-life onset require a broad medical evaluation.

Part 5 — Delirium Versus Primary Psychiatric Illness

Delirium is acute, fluctuating disturbance in attention and awareness with an underlying physiologic cause. It is common with infection, medication toxicity, withdrawal, hypoxia, metabolic disturbance, organ failure, and neurologic disease. Inattention, altered level of consciousness, abrupt onset, and fluctuation favor delirium over a primary psychiatric disorder.

Acute confusion is a medical emergency until proven otherwise. Do not attribute a sudden cognitive change in an older or medically ill patient to “anxiety” or “dementia” without assessment.

Part 6 — Substance-Related Presentations

Ask directly and nonjudgmentally about alcohol, opioids, sedatives, stimulants, cannabis, nicotine, prescribed medications, supplements, and timing of last use. Intoxication, withdrawal, overdose, and medication interactions can cause anxiety, depression, insomnia, agitation, psychosis, seizures, arrhythmia, respiratory depression, or delirium.

Safety depends on vital signs, consciousness, respiratory status, seizure risk, co-ingestants, and access to support. Severe withdrawal, overdose concern, impaired consciousness, or respiratory compromise requires emergency care.

Part 7 — Suicide-Risk Assessment and Immediate Safety

Ask directly about suicidal thoughts, desire to die, intent, plan, access to lethal means, past attempts, self-harm, substance use, agitation, hopelessness, psychosis, and protective supports. Asking does not create suicidal thoughts; it creates an opportunity for a truthful safety assessment.

Imminent risk includes current intent, plan with available means, inability to collaborate on safety, severe intoxication/psychosis, recent serious attempt, or inability to maintain safety. Do not leave a patient at imminent risk alone; activate emergency evaluation according to local protocol. In the U.S., 988 provides crisis support; life-threatening emergencies require emergency services.

Part 8 — FNP Assessment and Disposition

Obtain collateral information with appropriate consent when feasible, review medications, assess sleep and functioning, screen for trauma and interpersonal violence, and complete focused medical examination/testing when indicated. Consider pregnancy, thyroid disease, anemia, B12 deficiency, infection, sleep disorders, seizures, medication adverse effects, and substance use based on the presentation.

Outpatient care requires stability, no imminent safety risk, ability to follow a plan, timely follow-up, and a clear crisis/safety plan. Emergency psychiatric or medical evaluation is appropriate for suicidal/homicidal intent, grave disability, severe mania, acute psychosis with unsafe behavior, delirium, intoxication/withdrawal danger, or medical instability.

Part 9 — FNP Clinical Reasoning Case 1

A 44-year-old reports depression but also describes a prior week with almost no sleep, pressured speech, risky spending, and grandiosity. Reasoning: this is not automatically unipolar depression; assess for bipolar-spectrum illness, safety, substances, psychosis, and urgent psychiatric input.

Part 10 — FNP Clinical Reasoning Case 2

An 81-year-old develops sudden agitation, visual misperceptions, fluctuating attention, and a new fever. Reasoning: acute fluctuating inattention suggests delirium; evaluate for medical causes and arrange urgent care rather than diagnosing a primary anxiety disorder.

Part 11 — FNP Clinical Reasoning Case 3

A patient says, “Everyone would be better without me,” has been giving away possessions, drinks more heavily, and has access to a firearm. FNP decision: conduct immediate suicide-risk assessment, do not leave the patient alone if imminent risk is present, address lethal-means safety, and activate emergency/crisis resources.

FNP High-Yield Framework

Acute behavior/cognition change → first rule out delirium, intoxication/withdrawal, and medical instability.
Depression → assess function, bipolar history, substances, and suicide risk.
Psychosis/mania → assess safety, medical causes, capacity, and need for emergency psychiatric evaluation.
Suicide risk → ask directly about ideation, intent, plan, means, history, and protections; imminent risk requires emergency action.
